messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing a psychological case vignette
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

Write a realistic clinical case vignette for a patient with PTSD.
The vignette should read as a cohesive, flowing portrait — not a structured report.
Weave together who this person is, what happened to them, how they experience their
symptoms day to day, how they cope, and what toll this takes on their life and relationships.


Do not use section headers, numbered points, or clinical labels for symptoms.
Write 200–300 words in third person.
Cover: presenting complaints, trauma background, cognitive distortions, avoidance, and maintaining factors.
Avoid excessive jargon - write for a clinical case conference audience.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient presenting with PTSD.
Patient demographics:
- Age: 33
- Gender: Male
- Ethnicity: African
- Relationship Status: Single
- Occupation: Tailor
- Trauma Type: Terrorism
- Pcl5: 79

For the past several weeks, he has been coming to session straight from his workbench, still wearing the small remnant of a brightly colored thread on his cuff. He is a tailor by trade, a skill he learned as a teenager from his uncle back home in a bustling West African market town. His hands move with a precision that seems almost unconscious when he describes his work—cutting, pinning, stitching—but lately those hands have begun to tremor when he hears a sudden noise. He tells me, with a half-smile that does not reach his eyes, that he has been making mistakes on the seams of a wedding dress for a client who is due to pick it up next week. The client is angry. He cannot bring himself to redo the work. He just stares at the mannequin in his small rented shop, the measuring tape hanging limp around his neck.

The trauma happened two years ago, on a dry Saturday afternoon. He had been at the central market, walking between stalls of dyed fabric and metal buttons, searching for a specific shade of indigo. There was a loud crack—he first thought it was a car backfiring—then another, and another. Then the screaming. A man in a long coat had detonated a device near the bus station. He remembers the smell: burnt rubber, iron, and something sweet he cannot name. He remembers the wet warmth on his face that was not his own blood. He ran, leaving his bag of fabric behind. For days afterward he could not sew. His hands would not hold the needle steady.

Now, in the present, he lives in a quiet flat above his shop in a small city far from that market. He moved here eight months ago, hoping distance would silence the memories. It has not. Every afternoon, around the same hour, the sound of a motorcycle backfiring on the street below sends him dropping to the floor of his shop, heart hammering, the bolt of cloth he was measuring spilling across the linoleum. He stays there, crouched, until the silence returns and the shame rises. He no longer opens his shop on Saturdays. He tells clients he is closed for religious reasons, but he knows it is because that day remains soaked in dread.

Sleep is a battlefield. He dreams of the market, but in the dream the man in the coat is always someone he knows—a neighbor, a customer, his own reflection. He wakes gasping, drenched in sweat, and paces the small room until dawn. He has stopped answering calls from his family back home. His mother’s voice, worried and pleading, only makes him feel hollow and guilty. He lost the ability to feel close to anyone after that day. He dates occasionally, but when a woman touches his arm gently in a café, he flinches. He tells himself he is broken, that he does not deserve softness.

At the sewing machine, his concentration fractures constantly. A snippet of conversation outside, a sudden laugh—and his mind is back in the market, the panic flooding his chest. He has made three costly errors this month alone: cutting a suit jacket on the wrong grain, misaligning a zipper, forgetting to reinforce a hem. His regular customers have started murmuring. He feels watched, judged. He wonders if they can smell the fear on him.

He came to therapy because a friend from his mosque insisted, but he does not believe it will help. He holds his hands clasped tightly in his lap during our sessions, thumb rubbing thumb, as if trying to smooth a wrinkle he cannot see. When I ask him what he wants, he looks out the window and says, very quietly, "I want to stop jumping at shadows. I want to finish the wedding dress."
